title: Do you know what an ouroboros is?
short_title: The snake that comes full circle.
deck: A snake eating its own tail sounds like the end of a game. In an ancient symbol, it can mean a new beginning.
alt: Historic drawing of a scaled serpent forming a circle with its tail in its mouth
caption: An ouroboros drawn by Theodoros Pelecanos in 1478. This is historical artwork, not a photograph of a living snake.
body:
You might have heard a name like “Oroboro.” The symbol we’re exploring is usually called the ouroboros: a snake, or sometimes a dragon, curving around until its mouth meets its own tail.

A picture with no obvious beginning

Follow the creature around the circle. Where does it start? Where does it finish? That is part of the idea. The University Museum at the University of Tokyo describes the symbol as expressing ideas including infinity and repeated renewal. It is a picture people have used to think about cycles.

One symbol, different stories

Its meaning depends on where you find it. Yale’s exhibition on Egypt describes an old text, Hieroglyphica, that used the tail-eating serpent to represent the universe. A Greek manuscript of that work was rediscovered in 1419, and later translations helped its imagery travel through European art.

So it is more than a strange snake drawing. It is an example of how one simple image can hold a very big question.

The Snake-game connection

In our game, meeting your own tail ends the round. In an ouroboros, that meeting completes the circle. Same shape, very different idea!
question: What other things go in cycles—seasons, water, or something you noticed today?
sources: University of Tokyo University Museum · What is Ouroboros?

title: Meet the Maquech: this jewel-covered beetle is alive!
short_title: Maquech: this jewel-covered beetle is alive!
deck: Yes, it’s alive! In a tradition from Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, a living Maquech beetle is decorated and worn as jewellery.
alt: A living Maquech beetle decorated with colourful ornaments and attached to a chain
caption: This Maquech is a living beetle, decorated to be worn as jewellery. The ornaments are attached to its outside; they do not grow there naturally.
body:
Imagine a brooch that starts walking. A maquech, also spelled makech, is a real beetle that has been used as living jewellery. Its decorations are attached to its body, rather than embedded inside it.

A beetle beneath the sparkle

The Natural History Museum in London identifies the maquech as Zopherus chilensis, a flightless beetle. Its undecorated body has brown, grey and black markings that help it blend into bark covered with lichens.

The museum connects the jewellery tradition to Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. Its collection includes a nineteenth-century example decorated and attached to a chain.

Why the tiny chain?

Because the “jewel” has legs. The University of Colorado Museum describes a specimen adorned with ribbon and an opalescent material, with a chain that could be pinned to clothing. The chain connects the living insect to its wearer.

A question worth asking

The Colorado museum asks visitors to think about the boundary between a pet and an accessory. Learning about a tradition can also make us curious about an animal’s needs. We can appreciate the story without decorating a beetle ourselves.
question: How would you design beetle-inspired jewellery that leaves the living beetle in its habitat?
sources: University of Colorado Museum · Living Jewelry

title: A firefly is actually a beetle.
short_title: Breaking news: the firefly is a beetle.
deck: Those little lights in the evening belong to a family of beetles—and the glow is chemistry at work.
alt: Close-up photograph of a common eastern firefly showing its dark wing covers and reddish markings
caption: A common eastern firefly, Photinus pyralis. In daylight, its beetle body is easier to see; this photo does not show its glow.
body:
The name gives us a little puzzle: a firefly is a beetle in the family Lampyridae. “Lightning bug” is another name for the same kind of insect.

A light made by a living thing

The glow is called bioluminescence. Smithsonian Ocean explains that fireflies make light through a chemical reaction in their abdomens. Similar light-making abilities turn up in ocean life too, including some squid and tiny crustaceans.

For fireflies, the light-making part of the abdomen is wonderfully named the lantern. The National Park Service describes a reaction involving luciferin, an enzyme called luciferase, oxygen and other ingredients.

The flashes can be messages

Many fireflies use light to find and communicate with a mate. Some species glow steadily; some blink. Some do not produce light at all.

At Congaree National Park, one species, Photuris frontalis, is known for flashing together. That does not mean every firefly in every garden is part of a synchronized show.

A name isn’t a classification

Common names tell stories. Scientists look more closely to work out how animals are related. “Firefly” is a lovely name—but “beetle” tells us something different.
question: Can you think of another animal whose name might trick you about what it is?
sources: National Park Service · Synchronous Fireflies at Congaree

title: In England, a ladybug is called a ladybird.
short_title: Ladybug or ladybird? Same little neighbour.
deck: A familiar spotted insect has different everyday names on opposite sides of the Atlantic. And yes, it is a beetle too.
alt: A red seven-spot ladybird with black spots resting on a green leaf
caption: A seven-spot ladybird, Coccinella septempunctata, resting on a leaf.
body:
If a friend in England points out a ladybird, you do not need to look for a bird in a tree. They may be pointing to the little insect you call a ladybug.

One insect, two everyday names

Cambridge Dictionary labels ladybird as the UK term and ladybug as the US term. So the difference reaches beyond England: it is a difference in varieties of English. Neither name means we are talking about a different family of insects.

Another member of the beetle club

The Natural History Museum places ladybirds in the beetle family Coccinellidae. That means our firefly story and our ladybird story have a family resemblance: both are about beetles, though they belong to different beetle families.

And ladybirds are more varied than the classic red-and-black picture suggests. The museum describes harlequin ladybirds with red, orange and even black backgrounds, and different spot patterns.

Look past the familiar picture

A common name is a starting point, not the whole story. Next time you spot a ladybird, notice its colours and pattern. A careful observation can be the beginning of a new question.
question: What is this insect called in another language or in your family?
author: tmrCEO curiosity desk
